utterances.text: And you conclude this from the fact that, during the period, General Markac was based in Plitvice, and that was from 6th September to 13th September, the reports were still submitted in the same format from Gracac. That is it the basis for your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not on the same page there. It is my conclusion that the report was always -- reports were always sent out with his signature, irrespective of his whereabouts, be it Gracac or Plitvice. As far as I know, at a point in time when General Markac was at Plitvice, the reports were being sent from Plitvice, not from Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So then how do you include that, irrespective of where General Markac is, the reports would go out on a systematic basis, if, in fact, when he is in Plitvice the reports are sent out from Plitvice, and when he is in Gracac the reports are sent out from Gracac? What is the basis for you to include that reports went out even in the absence of General Markac when, in fact, they had been sent out from the location where he was at a given time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be clearly seen from the reports. Every report that was sent to the Main Staff as the operations were conducted on a day-to-day basis had the same format and had Mr. Markac's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So because the reports are in the same format and it bears General Markac's signature, you conclude that they're just sent in a systematic basis without General Markac getting involved in the reporting process, because of the format being the same? Is that how I understand your testimony to be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nowhere did I state that General Markac didn't see the reports; however, I cannot confirm that over the course of these two months, Mr. Markac was always in Gracac and that he wasn't in Zagreb, in Knin, or elsewhere. I cannot confirm that either. There are several handwritten reports which were sent, for instance, to Mr. Soljic. And on the basis of these reports, I can, again, presume that Mr. Markac was not at the staff but that it was somebody else who drafted the reports in the customary way and sent them on. I can tell you that this was the standard procedure that I used and other used in relation to the documents sent out from my department or the administration. The reports always bore my signature, although I didn't always sign them because I wasn't physically present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking about who drafted the reports, General. You have made a conclusion here that reports went out irrespective of where General Markac was, without his intervention. If could you clarify one question: Are you saying that General Markac did not see the report, there were times when he did not see the reports, or what exactly are you trying to say there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at no point did I say that General Markac didn't see them. I could not, because I wasn't there. What I wanted to say was that by comparing the documents that I had, and these were handwritten reports of action commanders and other participants, in view of the fact that the report was sent encoded or encrypted to the Main Staff -- or, rather, there were no differences or discrepancies between the handwritten reports and the latter reports that were sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you referred to, I think, before you say -- at page 52, you say: "I cannot confirm that either. There are several handwritten reports which were sent, for instance, to Mr. Soljic. And on the basis of these reports, I can, again, presume that Mr. Markac was not at the staff but that it was somebody else who drafted the reports in the customary way and sent them on." What are these reports that gave you an indication that Mr. Markac wasn't at a given -- at Gracac at the time the reports were sent out? What are these reports you are referring to? Have you cited them in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that some of the reports that were drafted were addressed to other persons, not solely to General Markac. Can I just have your question again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was asking you as to what these reports were that you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to the tell the Trial Chamber what those reports are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely which dates these were. But there were several handwritten reports sent both to Mr. Soljic or -- that's to say, also to Mr. Soljic. I don't have them here. But if you want, I don't think it would be difficult to try and obtain them. The reason why I didn't cite these documents was due to the fact that the final report that was ultimately drafted did not differ from these earlier reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. General Repinc, do you agree that during the period General Markac was in Plitvice, and that was 6th September to 13th September, all reports for that period were issued from Plitvice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the headquarters was there, I can only presume that nobody else could have draft the reports, save for Mr. Markac, and send it to the Main Staff. Now, was there a direct communication link between the Plitvice HQ and the Main Staff or whether the document was sent via Gracac, that's something I cannot confirm. Even if the documents stated something else, the reports could only have been written at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that all reports, the daily reports, were sent under General Markac's hand. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports I saw, which were sent every day, bore his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have document 3D00742, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is a document you have referred to at footnote 236 of your report, expert report, General. And you will see that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's 3D00742, 65 ter. It's a Defence 65 ter number. Now, I think you have probably got the wrong. That's the -- if you could just go right down the page, please. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this is the report sent on 13th September, General, for the activity of 13th September. And you can see from there that it's signed by the -- by Mr. Tomislav -- certainly not sent under General Markac's hand. Now, do you agree with me that this report reflects that when reports were sent in General Markac's absence by somebody else, in fact, that fact is reflected on the document itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misinterpreted the document. In this document, the subordinate officer, the commander of the Licko-Sinjska police unit, was sending the report to General Markac and not to the Main Staff. So we're talking about two different levels. This is the standard procedure when it came to communication between those who took part in daily searches, and, in this case, the chief of the sector at Plitvice, who, in turn, compiled these reports into one report, which then, bearing General Markac's signature, was sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you come across a report from General Markac sent on 13th September? Because this is the document you have cited as the daily report for 13th September.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was everything that I was able to find for the day. I wasn't able to find a document that would have gone from the special police sector to the chief of the Main Staff. So I repeat, the reports that were sent - and I believe that in relation to one of these days, I said that there -- a report was not sent to the chief of the Main Staff. So the reports that were sent to the Chief of the Main Staff, all of them had General Markac's signature. What I wanted to say in my expert report was that on this particular day, something did happen. In other words, searches were conducted in the way described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is not in evidence but cited in the expert report. Now, I -- I could tender it into evidence, but there are so many documents cited in the expert report which have not been tendered into evidence so I don't know what exactly the approach the Trial Chamber would take with regard to documents cited in the report which are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was our intention do submit all the documents which were not entered into the evidence during the testimony of expert witness in a form of bar table. So it is up to my learned colleague whether she wants to enter these documents separately. I have nothing against it, and I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it would -- it would not be a good idea to have them -- I mean, rather have them in a bar table document than in the usual way with the relevance and the possible comments of the Prosecution on the matter, then we keep everything together and we keep it manageable. So, therefore, Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that Mr. Mikulicic's observation will discourage you from, at this moment, tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I would like to take you to your report, paragraph 207, and that's where you report on the manner in which search operations were conducted by the special police forces. And in paragraph 207 you say: "Over the course of almost two months of activity, the collective forces staff developed a standard procedure for the conduct of search of terrain. It essentially consisted of several steps." And I won't go through all of steps. But in step two - this is just a clarification that I require. About the sixth line you say: "Information on enemy groups and mines and explosives were gathered by internal over-site personnel from the operative duty staffs of the -- of the police units, police department, Ministry of Interior, or the relevant Croatian army HQs." Now, that's a reference to the internal control sector of the special police sector, isn't it, the Inner Control Department of the Special Police Sector. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then, in step 4 to step 7, you describe - and it's also described further in paragraph 262 to 266 - you describe the reporting chain on search operations, and you set out the four levels. The first level being the group commanders; the second level, unit commander; third level, the operation commander; and the fourth level is General Markac. And this is what you say about that reporting chain at transcript 26768. You say: "The important thing is that it was, in fact, adhered to. Adhered to the way it has been described. It was known to everyone, and this was the way it was implemented from the point when addition was made of the fact that something needed to be searched to the point when, as the final step in the search, a report was sent to the chief of the Main Staff on the searches conducted during the day." Now, based on this -- and you further elaborate at transcript pages 26769 up to 71. Now, based on the reporting chain, as describe, General Markac's source of information on a particular operation for that day was -- was the operation commander, who commanded the operation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operation commander collected information from unit commanders, who, in turn, collected these from group commanders. It was up to the operation commander to deal with the information, be it by drafting the report with unit commanders right after the operation or later on at Gracac, but it was up to him to draft a report, the operation commander. And he would then forward the report either to General Markac or to the Main Staff. I -- I can't be sure about the latter part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, have you ever -- did you ever see a single report going from the operation commander directly to the Main Staff bypassing General Markac? Did you come across any such situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never came across such a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, therefore, if General Markac wanted any clarifications regarding a particular operation or wanted further information regarding an operation, he would have to revert to the operation commander. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 258, if I could take you to that page 258 of your report, in the conclusions, you report as follows: "After Operation Storm, during the period beginning on 13th August and concluding on 9th October, 1995, over 5.000 square kilometres of territory were examined in field searches." And you, you know, go on to describe it further and then say: "In two separate incidents, eight persons were killed while the special police sustained no casualties." And then in paragraph 259 you say: "The command system and operating methodology were fully developed and facilitated efficient mop-up and search operations. The two incidents which occurred on two consecutive days by the same unit should not lead to the erroneous conclusion that the system did not function and that undisciplined behaviour was tolerated." Now, what -- if I could just also add, in testimony you said this at transcript page 26772. You said: "We saw that the two incidents occurred on the 25th and the 26th. That is to say, four days into the search operation. We saw that the unit involved was the same in both incidents, and we saw that neither before nor after the two incidents did other incidents occur." Now, as you understand those incidents to be, what do you -- how do you -- at least what was the information that you received as the incidents that occurred on 25th and 26th that you say should not lead to any conclusion that the special police command tolerated indiscipline? What are those two incidents? And we know the dates, we, in fact, know it's a Grubori incident and another incident on the 26th. But what really happened as you understand it to be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, I should like to make a correction of my expert report, because I somehow managed to tie up two incidents mentioned in 258 and 259 in an erroneous way. What I wanted to say is that it shouldn't be concluded that the two incidents on the 25th and the 26th resulted in the death of eight persons. Where the death of eight persons is mentioned, this is in relation to a report on the 23rd of August, 1995, where it was recorded that the special police unit of the Splitsko-Dalmatinska Police Administration -- or the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration destroyed a terrorist group consisting of three armed individuals. So these were the three persons plus the five victims of the Grubori incident. I wanted to mention this for the sake of precision. As for the two incidents, based on what I read in the documents sent by General Markac to the Main Staff, one of the two was the Grubori incident on the 25th, resulting in the death of five individuals, and the incident on 26th in the village of Ramljane, where a number of houses were burned, a number of houses and other structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you also see any documentation which indicated to you that in the course of the operation on 25th, where five persons were killed, that 20 houses and several farm buildings also were burnt?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I'm referring to, for the record, P764. Did you receive any documents or review any documents which showed you that houses were burnt and barns were burnt on the 25th also?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw any new documents. I saw the reports produced on the 26th. I saw the written report by the action commander, Mr. Janic. I saw a report that was written on the basis of this and sent to the Main Staff. I suppose it was sent there, although the report had the word to be made null and void on it. And I also saw another report produced on the 26th and sent to the chief of the Main Staff where it was stated that certain clashes occurred. That's to say, armed clashes with the enemy forces, causing casualties and the burning of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, General Repinc, you say that these two incidents should not lead to the conclusion that discipline was tolerated by the special police command -- special police sector command. Are you aware that no member of the special police units had been disciplined for those two incidents, to date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I'm aware, there are certain pending proceedings in Croatia, in relation to these cases. Since the reports were made as they were, with the formulations they had, I did not go into analysing what had, indeed, transpired there, whether there were conflicts or clashes or not, because such an inquiry would require, me to engage in conversations with a number of participants in these events. And I did not want to base my report on interviews or any other form of cooperation with the participants in these events. I wanted to base my report solely on documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, you just mentioned there are certain pending proceedings in Croatia in relation to these cases. Are you referring to the fact that just last month - and that's the latter half December 2009 - Mr. Sacic, the chief of staff of the special police, and members of the special police -- the Lucko Unit were arrested by the Croatian authorities in relation to the crimes in Grubori. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Chamber informed about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there has been a formal intimation about this. We have called for the official documentation from Croatia, and we have still not received it. Once those documents are received, we will tender them to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether -- I don't know what these documents are, if these are -- it may cause some technical problems as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the documents we have called for the -- the investigation documents as well as the court proceedings in relation to the -- the arrest of these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will wait and see what you will present to the Court, under what circumstances, and under what -- Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we are on this topic, Your Honour, I would like to inform the Chamber that the Markac Defence also requested the documents, which is -- concern the investigation of Grubori case, and we were rejected officially by the county court in Zagreb with the explanation that they are not obliged to provide us the documents but only to the ICTY and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think no request has been received by this Chamber to -- at this moment to give support in obtaining any such documents which -- let me be -- be quite transparent. This Chamber receives, on a regular basis, summaries of press publications. We do not receive that as a Chamber, but we just receive by e-mail a coverage of what is published in the local press. Therefore, if it is relevant for our case, we usually close our eyes and wait what comes up in court because that's where everyone can see what reaches us. At the same time, I would not hide from the parties that the Judges of this Chamber have shared with each other that they saw some of these press reports and that they were wondering whether, what apparently is investigated, whether sooner or later, in whatever form, it would be informed, but then in a more thorough way, about the results of such investigations, which are apparently focussing on at least the same events as is a relevant event for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think it's better that we -- when I asked, Is the Chamber informed about it, of course, I did so because we were not informed about it officially. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood, obviously, much of this happened right toward the end of the session and during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Court should be aware and Chamber should be aware we obviously tried to get this information on our own. And since we were rejected, we will be seeking the Court' intervention in obtaining this information. So we thought we would take the first step and try to get this cooperatively. And since we have been rejected, we will be asking for the Court's support. So I don't know if the Prosecution wishes to do so the same, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that if the Prosecution would receive such material, that it would -- it would be under the general disclosure -- I cannot say yet not knowing anything about it, whether it will be exculpatory or in any other way. But I take it there will be full disclosure of material that seems to -- at least at first sight, may have some relevance for the case before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, now, your testimony was that the -- the search operations carried during the period 21st August to 3rd October were not clearing operations but they were search operations. In that -- what the forces expected to meet at this stage were just small groups, if at all, of, you know, residue, enemy forces and not large, you know, enemy forces. Is that -- isn't -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your testimony is - and this is at transcript page 26746 going to 47 - that: "In the case of search operations, the forces would carry light weaponry, as there was no expectation to meet strong resistance." Now you have reviewed these reports and you have seen that on two consecutive dates where the same unit was involved, several houses and structures caught fire. Now, you're an officer with a substantial amount of military experience. Did you query or did you wonder as to how so many houses could catch fire in the course of two days in -- on two consecutive days when, in fact, the forces were carrying light weaponry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking of light weaponry, I wish we could be more precise. I don't know what you mean precisely when you say that. Light weaponry, to me, means that an individual can carry it in his arms or on his back. It could include infantry weapons or light armour weapons. If they had such weapons, I don't know what the reason for that may have been. But, by the same token, I cannot say that they wouldn't take them if ordered to. In any case, I don't know for certain what the units searching the area had. During a customary, ordinary search, such units would have such weapons which could be carried around without imposing undue burden. Given that they were supposed to search some difficult terrain, and given that they had to cover large distances, that would be my conclusion. How and why the houses were burnt down and how it came about that there was such a number of them, that is something I can't say because I wasn't there. And I don't know the conditions of those operations and why there was burning in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. If I could take you to paragraph 218 of your report. And this is at page 91 of the report. Actually, your paragraph 218 starts at page 91, but the portion I want read to you is at page 92. This is about the tenth line you refer to the -- the incident in Grubori. You say: "45 members from Lucko anti-terrorist unit" -- I'm sorry, it's the next paragraph. "According to the first report, no hostilities with residual enemy formations occurred during search operations." And you cite General Markac's first report sent in relation to this day's activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is P575, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "The reports submitted to the chief of General Staff was drafted on the basis of a handwritten report by the operational commander, the head of the anti-terrorism department, Zdravko Janic." And this is -- you cite, in support of that, at footnote 188, Mr. Janic's report which is P560. Now, it's correct, isn't it, that according to the reporting chain that you described, the standard procedures, that the operation commander's report and General Markac's report to the chief of the General Staff should be consistent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, that the report sent to the chief of the Main Staff, was drafted based on the handwritten report of Mr. Janic. In other words, Mr. Janic was not the one sending the report. The report that eventually reached the Main Staff by electronic communication means was put together based on his handwriting report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then you go on to say in that same paragraph: "Based on new information, an amended report was submitted to the GS HV General Staff on hostilities in the village of Grubori during which five persons were killed." And you give a description of what's in that second report. And you cite General Markac's second report at footnote 189.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record it's P576.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you say that P576 has been drafted based on new information. What is the new information that, according to the documents you reviewed for information, that General Markac had which led him to cancel his first report, P575, and submit the second report, P576?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot say what prompted General Markac to change the report. In any case, it was. What I must say, though, is that I was unable to come up with the new changed report of the operation commander, which would be written the same way as the original. I didn't see a handwritten report by Mr. Janic based on which one could arrive at the new report. In any case, the new report was obviously made, as stated here. Since the amended report was made, obviously, in the meantime, some new information reached General Markac and the joint forces staff to the effect that the information provided in the first report was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as I understand what you're saying, General, you're -- since this amended report was made, you're speculating that General Markac had information that led to him creating a new -- a second report. There is no factual basis for you to assert that there was new information. Is that correct? You're speculating.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat this. If someone asked for a new report, it must mean that there was some new information which General Markac did not have at the time of the original report. But as to who, why, and how made this, and based on -- based on what, that is something I cannot say, because that would take me to the realm of investigative measures for which I was not competent. I could not question people on what was taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, you said that you couldn't find a handwritten report of Mr. Janic. I can tell you that is because there is no second report issued by General, by Mr. Janic which supports General Markac's second report. In fact, Mr. Janic testified in these proceedings to that effect. Now that you have been made privy to that fact, would you find it a matter of concern that General Markac would forward an amended report on this incident when it is not supported by a report from the operational commander, which breaches the -- the reporting chain that you have described in your report, expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't listen to what Mr. Janic said. I don't know whether there is such a report or not. What I said is that I was unable to find it in the documents I had at my disposal. Taking all the other facts into account, I don't know how it came about that the follow-up report was made. Therefore, I can't say that this would be an area of concern or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, could I ask you one question. Earlier you said there must have been new information because there was a new report. Now, could you explain what is the compelling logic behind this observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My reasoning went along the lines that if Mr. Janic drafted and sent his report and if General Markac received it as such and sent it onto the chief of the Main Staff, then there was no need to send a new report, unless, in the meantime, there was some new information based on which he based the new report. Again, I am unable to say what information that was and where it came from, but someone had to know something different in relation to what had been written in the first report, and that someone must have acquainted General Markac with it. It was based on that, that the new report was made, based on that information. This is my military logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you considered the possibility that in the second report not new factual information but, for example, just invented facts were produced and apparently you are excluding that. Could you tell us on the basis of what you could exclude that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never said that it excludes that possibility. As I said, General Markac sent reports, based on what he received from the operation commander, meaning that all the reports he sent to the Main Staff contained information he received from his subordinates, some of which may have been incorrect. This brings us to the issue of the commander and his relation with his subordinates. And it touches upon certain areas which should be incorporated into any policeman's everyday work and that policeman's relation to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. Well, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether -- repeating my invitation to proceed. Could you give us a time indication, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is a good time, Mr. President, to take the break, and I will finish within the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I'll just ask two more questions on that subject that we were discussing, that's the Grubori incident, and move on to a new area. Now, when you reviewed the reports relating to the action on 25th August, you reviewed the operation commander's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is P560 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And General Markac's first report, P575, which do not contain any reference whatsoever to the Lucko Unit meeting with resistance in the course of the operation, or there is no reference to any incident of whatever nature. Both record that there was no fire contact and no material found. And then you reviewed General Markac's second report, P576, which contains quite an elaborate description of the Lucko Unit being involved in a conflict. There are civilians killed, enemy soldiers killed, houses on fire, and weapons found. So did you query in your mind, was it a matter of concern that there is such a huge departure from the first report to the second report on the same operation? Did you wonder how this could happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As with all other reports and documents, each and every document I had before me is something I analysed, in terms of its contents. In that sense, comparing the two documents, I did notice the departure. As a person, of course, I was interested in it, and I would have been happy to have been able to know what, indeed, happened. However, given the nature of this touchy issue which is still under investigation, I did not undertake any investigation on my part, in order to ascertain what happened and why.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could I ask a follow-up question here. You said the matter was still under investigation. But when you published the report, what was your knowledge about any ongoing investigation at that time? When you drafted your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no specific knowledge, except for what I could learn from the newspapers. And that is that certain people, headed by Mr. Sacic, were brought into custody and that they were in the investigative prison being questioned about the Grubori events. Except for what I could read in the papers, I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you explain -- you were asked what came to your mind when you studied these documents. And then you said you noticed the departure; you were interested in it; and however, given the nature of the touchy issue, which is still under investigation - apparently, there was no knowledge of any investigation going on when you drafted your report, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning Grubori, most people in Croatia, including myself, know the story, because it keeps appearing in the press. And it is constantly being referred to as a case that still hasn't been shed any light on, and that there are investigations ongoing. In order for me to sled any light on it, I would have to have all the ability and authority and instruments that this Tribunal has at its disposal to be able to investigate the case in any further detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are called as an expert witness to analyse documents. Now, Ms. Mahindaratne asks you, What came to your mind? Because it -- well, the one information says this; the other information says that; the report which gives a quite different explanation. And then to say, Well, it's a very sensitive issue. I'd rather not -- I mean, you could at least, instead of saying, Well, there must have been new information, you could have said, Well, this -- without knowing exactly what new information there was, I cannot explain this; or there is an flaw in the information I have available to assess whether or not there was any new information. I mean, that's on the basis of the analysis of the documentation. But now to say, Well, we all know that it's a sensitive issue. I mean, you, as an expert witness, you are studying the documents and you are drawing conclusions. So -- and then you say, Well, in view of the investigations ongoing, where, at the time, when you drafted the report, there was, at least, from what this Chamber knows, there was no publications on any intensified or ongoing investigation. And then to say, Well, let the Tribunal find out. You're here to assist us to find out. And, therefore, we expect an analysis, a critical an analysis of everything you find. Would you please -- and perhaps I take you back to something that happened before, today, whether or not Mr. Markac arrived at one minute past 10.00 or not in Gracac, the Chamber expects from an expert to say, Well, we found this information which is contradicted by that information, and for these and these reason, I conclude that this information is most likely incorrect, rather than just drawing just general conclusions. I'm more or less asking you whether you agree with me on the role of an expert witness studying these documents. This was question was too long, but I give you an opportunity to -- to give any comments on what I just put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you. I apologise for perhaps being clumsy in terms of the wording I used. I'm unused to being in this seat. It is my omission, if I used inappropriate terminology. But what I could see in the documents is something that did not bring me to a definite conclusion as to why there was a change in the report and what it was caused by and what ultimately it means for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just one last question on this, General. At paragraph 259, specifically referring to the Grubori incident and the incident on 26th, you say: "The command system and operating methodology were fully developed and facilitated efficient mop-up and search operations. The two incidents which occurred on two consecutive days by the same units should not lead to the erroneous conclusion that the system did not function and that undisciplined behaviour was tolerated." Now, do you agree with me that you drew that conclusion without really analysing the facts and the -- the material relating to the two incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew that conclusion because the operation of searching and mopping up lasted between the 12th of August until the 9th of October, 1995. That is to say, over two months. During that period, with short interruptions, there were almost daily tasks, including hundreds of policemen, on a daily basis. During all those operations, with the exception of these two days involving the same unit, there were no other incidents I came across. This is what made me conclude that if such behaviour had been allowed and tolerated and had there been no one to address it, it is my presumption that the number of cases would have been far greater. We are speaking here of a single unit out of the group of 19 units and the two days involving that unit, if they did what is claimed. That is something that still needs to be determined.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, have you received any information about the evidence led in this Court about members of the special police being seen in Gracac in the -- in fact, centre of Gracac looting property? In fact, there have been photographs tendered into these proceedings. Have you been -- have you received that information or have you been privy to that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of it and that there is such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to object to the form of that question. I know it's been after the question has been asked and answered, but there is no evidence. There is accusations. I don't have if photograph that have been depicted in this case show actual people looting property. I think that's a pretty broad accusation to make without specific facts being given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm referring to the testimony of Mr. Vanderostyne. I think -- Mr. Mikulicic is nodding, perhaps Mr. Kuzmanovic has forgot than testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well then perhaps, Counsel, you could cite that testimony, instead of making broad accusations. We don't have to spend hours an hours on this, Your Honour, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. If you would have phrased it more cautiously, Ms. Mahindaratne, that is, evidence "suggesting" or evidence that could be "interpreted as," then you would have avoided that Mr. Kuzmanovic would have made these observations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, Mr. President, P321, the reference to Mr. Vanderostyne's testimony. Moving on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on, General. Now, during direct examination, and also examination of Mr. Kehoe, you discussed the JNA doctrine of the -- regarding the defence of populated areas. Now, in fact, you have discussed this doctrine under section 7.2.1 of your report which entitled: "The Enemy's Doctrine." And this is what you said in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's at transcript page 26706.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Referring to this particular doctrine you say: "I'd like to say that in the directive for defence which was issued by General Mrksic it says, for example, that the town of Knin must be prepared for the defence of this kind. And it even goes on to stipulate that for the defence of the town of Knin, a separate command be set up for the defence of the town itself." Now, what is the order you're referring to here, the directive of General Mrksic? Is it his directive issued on 5th of August? Is that what you were referring to? You know, I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't come across a directive that would have been issued on the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the directive then you are referring to? I'm drawing your attention to what you testified in direct examination. When you said this particular doctrine of defence of populated areas is also reflected in General Mrksic's directive. So what is that directive? We are aware of a directive issued on 5th August. Now, are you aware of any other -- anything else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I need to find the reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You've discussed, in fact, the doctrine, if you want to -- let me help assist you. At paragraph -- section 7.2.1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a directive for the use of the Serbian Army of Krajina from February of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which footnote are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's footnote 35. And then footnotes 36 and 37 refer to the same document and specifically items 4 and 5, items 4 and 5 of the document. So they're both referring to the same document but different parts thereof. So these are the specific references.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could have D944, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, your words were lost. Could you tell us ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But Ms. Mahindaratne obviously was able to hear it so she asked for the document that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber will stay out of this private conversation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is this the document you're referring to, General Repinc? You can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, you said that this document reflects the defence of populated areas. And you said that, in fact, this doctrine, based on this doctrine, you conclude that the RSK located military targets within populated areas. Can you please direct the Trial Chamber to the section in this document which supports your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4 of the decision states: "I have hereby decided," et cetera, et cetera. And goes on to mention the aggression with a limited objective and the aggression with a radical objective. At the end of page 8, operational deployment of forces is referred to. There, the forces for the control of territory are mentioned. Forces for the protection of buildings. Forces for clashes with sabotage and diversionary groups. And then forces for occupying urban-populated areas. It is stated that the IKM was set up in the area of Petrova Gora and command post in Knin. This is -- and further below, in item 5.11, the defence of towns is referred to, where it is stated that the focal point should be on the preparation of towns and populated areas; namely the town of Knin where --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just slow down, we are trying to follow this document. And can you just mention again the section where you said there was a defence of populated areas mentioned. What -- what paragraph was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's paragraph 5.11 at page 14. At the bottom, it is stated: "The defence of towns and large populated areas."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the paragraph of -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if could you keep -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So where in this paragraph, General, do you see any information that supports your conclusion that the ARSK located military targets within populated area? Is it the word "defence preparation of larger populated areas and towns for long-term and circular defence" that gave you that -- that assisted you in arriving at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance to the counsel and Chamber, there is another paragraph, to 5.11, that goes on to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, as I read it, it says: "Focus on the preparation of towns and populated areas on the frontlines and the preparation of the town of Knin for which a command and defence unit [sic] shall be established separately." Now, as I read it, it says "for the defence of Knin for which a command and defence unit [sic] shall be established separately." I don't read it as any military installations being located within unit. I mean, is that how you understood this document to be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody can prepare the defence of a town without having military targets placed in it. Well, the very army defending the town is the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, have you seen General Mrksic's order dated 5th August? You said you haven't seen it earlier on. I'm just making sure that you haven't seen it at all or you weren't talking about that document earlier. Have you seen an order of General Mrksic dated 5th August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have D1511, please. And in the English, if you could move to the next page, please, second page. Before that, please, I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, if you could just go to the first page. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, you might want to just take time to quickly review this. This is an order of General Mrksic issued on 5th August. And it says: "Urgent measures in order to stabilise defence, an order."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It reads: "7th corps with the 103rd Infantry Brigade is stabilising a defence along Mala Dinara-Derala-Otric-Malovan frontline by persistent defence with a goal to prevent the enemy taking Knin without being engaged in a battle and joining of the enemy forces which are engaged in directions Knin-Otric and Gracac. Otric, a part of the forces, is to continue the battle in the encirclement. One unit is to be sent to the area of Bulina Strana for the defence of the area of Knin and a prevention of the enemy's rapid advance towards Otric. Soldiers are to be separated from the refugees and returned to combat units under any circumstances. Command post is in the area of Otric. Support is provided by the artillery." Now, General do you read, here, anything in this document which indicates to you that the defence of the town of Knin included relocation of military targets within the town?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That -- we're talking about two different issues here. We're talking about a preparation for the defence of Knin prior to Operation Storm and events that took place subsequent to the Operation Storm commencing on the 4th of August. This -- pardon the -- the pedestrian analogy, but this is apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well then, for you, I will allow you to put questions to the witness in relation to this in order to sort it out. And, Ms. Mahindaratne, you are encouraged not to mix up apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Let me just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't say that this is what are you doing, but at least you are now aware that you are alleged of doing this by Mr. Kehoe at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take note of that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, General, do you, in this order, see any indication that there were military targets placed in Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Having been a member of the former Yugoslav army, I am aware of how these orders were written. I wrote them myself as part of my training. It is stated here that the 7th corps with the 1st Battalion of 103rd Infantry Brigade ought to do this and that. And then it goes on to say, With a following task: Persistent defence -- through persistent defence, prevent Knin from being taken. In other words, one need to -- needs to defend the town of Knin through persistent fighting. Where it is stated "without engaging in combat," this does not mean that the forces will not come into contact with the enemy forces. It is impossible to engage in defence without fighting. It is stated here that, through persistent defence, it is to be prevented -- or Knin is to be prevented from falling into the hands of the enemy. You cannot prevent Knin from falling into the enemy hands unless you are there and defending it. In other words, this means that there had to be a presence of the RSK soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused at this moment. Apparently Ms. Mahindaratne is talking about something quite different from what you are talking about. Ms. Mahindaratne is exploring, apparently, where you found sources which would indicate that military targets would be more or less hidden in populated areas. For example, not to say that this is an example, but on page 28 on the top there's something written about a depot to be put in a school building; whereas, you apparently are talking about something entirely different. Earlier you said, If you want to defend the town, that means that that defence, in itself is a military target. Now, I see that point. But I think these are two entirely different matters. The one is whether or not, if you want to defend the town, whether that means that the town or the whole of the town, or -- has become a military target. I take it that if troops are in the town that you could consider those troops to be a military target. If equipment would be in the town, that those could be military target -- that's quite different from putting a depot in a school or in a apartment block where civilians are living or whatever. I think that from the questions and from your answers, I get the impression that you're talking about different matters. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if I may, and if -- I think the confusion might have come from counsel's question on page 80, line 10 and 11, concerning military targets in Knin. And I trust, at this point in this proceeding, there is no debate that there were military targets. So if there was some confusion in this question and answer, it could very well have emanated from that particular question, which I think the witness -- well, I'm not going to speak for the witness. The witness says was he has said going from line 12 through line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that he's contributing, triggered by whatever, in the confusion as well. But I think we have almost a whole day to reconsider whether this confusion should continue or whether we should put an end to it. Ms. Mahindaratne, I am aware that quite some time was taken. You said you will finish in the next -- in the next session. I would still -- how much more time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes. Then we are not going to do that. May I take it that there will be a need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maximum ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions by any of the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, it depends where this latter portion of the inquiry goes. Even in that case, I don't anticipate too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that we would not continue at this very moment. We would finish it in -- after having given these subjects all the thoughts they need. You'd have another ten to 15 minutes tomorrow, Ms. Mahindaratne. And then we'll -- I would expect that we would finish certainly well within the first session tomorrow, which brings me also to my next question, but perhaps we already excuse Mr. Repinc. Mr. Repinc, we are unable to finish you today without rushing through the material, and that's not what the Chamber intends to do at this moment. It will not be for very long, but we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in another courtroom, Courtroom II. And I would like to instruct you again that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that's testimony given last week or today or still to be given tomorrow. But refrain from any conversations or any communications in relation to your testimony. You may follow the Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next witness, because there has been a request by the Cermak Defence to do housekeeping on -- not on Friday, Thursday is completely impossible for the Chamber, so I'd like to inquire as to how much time we need for the next witness to look at -- if is at all possible, to do the housekeeping on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. The Prosecution has less than one session cross-examination for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will -- I was expecting, at most two sessions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sessions. Other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Less than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I'll just reserve half an hour, but it might be less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, it's, therefore, highly uncertain whether we will be able to finalise a housekeeping session on Wednesday because we have now, at least, well into -- well, one session for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Less than one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than -- yes, I'm -- I have developed a professional scepticism about less than. I hope I will be forgiven for that. Less than one session. And then you as well, Mr. Mikulicic, two sessions, which makes -- certainly more than three taking everything together. Tomorrow, 45 minutes for the expert witness. More than three sessions would bring us well into Wednesday morning. And that's the reason why I say that it's uncertain. And there are a few other matters. There were two times ten minutes for further submissions in relation to witness interviews, which is also -- we postponed that last week. There's one other decision which I could postpone as reasons for protective measures. But I'm -- I'm a bit -- I'm -- I'm certain -- the Chamber certainly is supporting any -- any wish to see that we can do without Friday, but I can't give any guarantees as matters stand now at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, it's just that it ties up staff that could be working on other projects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I wanted the Court to understand that particularly where we have a gap in between and I have to juggle my troops and put them in various places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Keep them well under command and control, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do wish to be heard on the issue of the witness interviews, Your Honour. I know that there were submissions made by ten minutes on each side. I wouldn't need ten minutes, but I do want to be heard on that issue with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think both parties were given -- all parties to say that ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were very brief in your earlier written submissions, so perhaps there is good reason to -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. On this subject, I just wanted to advise you that we may need 15 minutes because the -- I think the Defence filing from the Gotovina Defence has been very substantial; I think more than 3.000 words. So that's what the Prosecution would need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're coming closer and closer to Friday. That's -- Mr. Misetic, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to correct the record, I don't believe our filing exceeded the word limit. I don't believe that that's the filing that exceeded the word limit. I believe there was one other filing, but it's unrelated to the issue that's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there was no suggestion that it was above the word limit but that it was a substantial submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the risk of getting in trouble with my colleagues for this afternoon, the Chamber has extended the time for Defence and Prosecution -- the dead-line to respond to Croatia's submissions in relation to the Chamber's invitation of the 18th of December, when I remember -- I remember that when we discussed this extension of time we had on our minds that we would like to receive them before the housekeeping session which was then still foreseen to take place on Friday. If we would even give it a try to do the housekeeping session on Wednesday, the Chamber would encourage the parties then to make their written submissions before that housekeeping session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I certainly would -- try to do that. But the presentation or the submission by Croatia, in conjunction with the Office of the Prosecutor, is extensive. And we plan on taking that on full board so to be given a full and complete response to the situation. It would be difficult, very difficult, to do and complete prior to that session. We will try our best, but it would be very difficult to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, you will understand that the Chamber is trying to clean its desk rather soon, and we'll see what is possible and what is not possible. Extension of time has been granted before the discussion on the housekeeping session on Friday was started. So, therefore, as matters stand now, I just encouraged you to do something, which is different from instructing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for doing this now, but just to put it on the Court's radar, we did file a motion on Tuesday concerning the European Union's failure to respond to the Chamber's invitation. I know that typically there's two weeks to file a response, but given the conclusion of the case, if we could expedite that procedure, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Chamber - I don't know whether that's yet on the record or not - received some information as -- in relation to the delay in receiving the request and that a response could be received in relatively short time from now, which might cause us not to engage in another round of -- and perhaps, first, wait from an answer. From what I remember, there was an indication that it would be within the next week or ten days. And it had got to do something with delays over the recess period. So this is already for your information. But we have not finally considered this matter, but we have seen your motion. Then I'll -- it took me a while, but we're now at a point to adjourn for the day. And we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 19th of January, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
